newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia condemns racism in report to U.N..
newsitem.headline: Australia condemns racism in report to U.N..

text.p: Australia has condemned racism as an attack on human dignity and security and a threat to world peace in a report to the United Nations general assembly, Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Thursday.

In its annual report to the United Nations on racism, Australia pledged its commitment to the abolition of racial discrimination and the government's commitment to denounce racism, Downer said in a statement released here.

"The government's support of U.N. processes to stop racial discrimination is complementary to our absolute commitment to maintaining a non-discriminatory immigration policy and a society free of the ugly stigma of racism," Downer said.

The report, presented on Wednesday, comes during a bitter and divisive debate in Australia over racism and immigration, sparked last month by independent politician Pauline Hanson's charge that the country was being swamped by Asians, and her call for a halt to immigration.
Asians make up about 4.7 percent of Australia's 18 million population and about one third of the nation's 100,000 immigrants each year.
Canberra's U.N. report cited Australia's strong record of ethnic harmony and a joint parliamentary motion last week condemning racism and supporting a tolerant society.
"Racism, in all its forms, constitutes a serious assault on human dignity and security," the statement to the United Nations said.
"Consequently, it remains a major source of conflict and poses a continuing threat to peace and stability throughout the developed and developing parts of the world," it said.
"Australia has a profound commitment to fair treatment for all and a harmonious blending together of people of different racial backgrounds.
"Its record of achievement in integration into a very harmonious and united people from all parts of the world is something of which all Australians can be immensely proud."
The racism debate and Prime Minister John Howard's refusal to repudiate Hanson's comments have been criticised by Asian media and prompted warnings Australia's relations with Asia were at risk.
